title: Combining whole-cell patch clamp and dye loading in acute brain slices with bulk RNA sequencing in embryonic to aged mice
protocol: Bubble the slicing aCSF with 95% O2 / 5% CO2 for at least 30 min (to set pH to 7.2–7.4), on ice.
Calibrate the vibratome blade according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Place the slicing chamber in the freezer for at least 5 min.
Once cooled, place the slicing chamber on the vibratome and fill the outer chamber with ice.
Fill the chamber with ice-cold slicing aCSF once it has been bubbled for 30 min.
Continuously bubble the slicing solution with 95% O2 / 5% CO2 until the last slice is cut to maintain pH throughout the procedure.
Cool two beakers (one 10 mL and one 50 mL) and a glass petri dish on ice.
Fill the resting chamber with slicing aCSF and continuously bubble it with 95% O2 / 5% CO2 until the end of the recording day.
Fill the two beakers with bubbled slicing aCSF after 30 minutes of bubbling.
Remove the head and immerse it in the 50 mL glass beaker containing bubbled slicing aCSF.
Cut the skin along the midline, exposing the skull.
Use the exposed skull to hold the head by folding the skin under the head.
Make a cut between the eyes.
Make lateral cuts in the skull from anterior to posterior.
Remove the skull.
Alternatively, make a cut near the midline above the hindbrain.
Peel off the skull above the brainstem and cerebellum.
Make lateral cuts in the skull above the forebrain from posterior to anterior.
Peel off the skull above the forebrain.
Carefully extract the brain using a small spatula.
Dip the spatula in slicing aCSF before use.
Immerse the brain in 10 mL glass beaker containing bubbled slicing aCSF.
Fill the glass petri dish with bubbled aCSF.
Transfer the brain into the petri dish using the large spatula.
Keep the petri dish on ice.
Optional: Dissect the meninges from postnatal brains.
Optional: Dissect the region of interest, such as the forebrain.
Optional: Fill one well in a 4-well plate halfway with melted agarose.
Place a dissected brain in the well and add more agarose to fill the well.
Ensure that the brain is correctly positioned for the required slice orientation (coronal/sagittal/transverse).
Repeat this procedure for each brain.
Place the plate on ice or in the fridge to allow the agarose to set rapidly.
Glue the brain to the vibratome slicing platform in the correct orientation.
Consult a brain atlas to determine the right slicing orientation.
Cut 225 μm–325 μm thick slices.
Transfer each slice into the resting chamber using the glass Pasteur pipette.
Allow the slices to rest for 1 hour before recording.
Prepare the pipettes and patch clamp set up for the day.
Fire-polish both ends of glass capillaries using a Bunsen burner.
Use the fire-polished capillaries to pull glass electrodes using an electrode puller.
For OPCs, recommend pulling electrodes with a 5–7 MΩ resistance.
Thaw an aliquot of internal solution and keep it on ice and protected from light.
Turn on all the electrical equipment.
Oxygenate the recording aCSF with 100% O2.
Start running the solutions through the gravity-fed perfusion.
Ensure that the lines are free of air bubbles.
Bubble the solutions throughout the recordings.
Transfer a slice from the resting chamber into the recording chamber using a glass Pasteur pipette.
Use a harp to hold the slice in position at the bottom of the recording chamber.
Locate the slice under the microscope with the 4/5× objective.
Identify the region of interest.
Switch to a 40×/63× immersion objective with IR-DIC optics.
Use fluorescence to identify reporter-expressing OPCs.
Switch back to brightfield to identify a good OPC.
Identify OPCs that appear smooth with a soft and clear outline.
Discard shiny cells with a hard outline as they are difficult to seal.
Avoid round cells with a visible nucleus as they are dying cells.
Alternate between fluorescence and brightfield to assess cell location accurately.
Avoid cells adjacent to blood vessels when using fluorescent reporters under the NG2 promoter.
Fill a glass pipette with internal solution and fit it in the electrode holder on the micromanipulator headstage so that the chlorided electrode is in contact with the internal solution.
Raise the objective so that it is still in contact with the bath solution, but there is enough space to lower the electrode into the bath.
Lower the electrode into the bath.
Apply ±5 mV (or 10 mV) voltage pulse every 30 ms for 15 ms duration.
Display the resulting current on your computer monitor using Clampex software.
Adjust the pipette offset current to zero on the amplifier.
Apply positive pressure to prevent debris from collecting at the tip of the electrode.
Find the electrode under the microscope.
Lower the electrode and objective until just above the cell of interest.
Increase the positive pressure as you approach the cell.
Switch from positive pressure to negative pressure when the electrode contacts the cell.
Set the holding potential to −60 mV on the amplifier.
Measure a junction potential of −14 mV between internal solutions and recording aCSF.
Correct for junction potential, ensuring that a holding potential of −60 mV on the amplifier corresponds to −74 mV.
Apply negative pressure until a giga-ohm seal is achieved.
Monitor resistance using Clampex, aiming for at least 1 GΩ.
Observe the reduction in current as evidence of a successful seal formation.
Adjust negative pressure for each cell based on the rate of resistance increase and current decrease.
Compensate pipette capacitance on the amplifier according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Apply short, hard, negative pressure pulses to open the cell.
Monitor for a membrane capacitive current in response to voltage pulses.
Observe Lucifer Yellow-containing internal solution within the cell.
Adjust negative pressure cautiously to prevent breaking the seal and discarding the cell.
Apply a 50 ms ± 5 mV voltage pulse.
Calculate Rs, membrane capacitance (Cm), and membrane resistance (Rm) from the applied voltage pulse.
Compensate series resistance (Rs) according to the manufacturer’s manual.
Monitor Rs throughout recording by regularly applying a 50 ms ±5 mV voltage pulse.
Discard cells with an Rs larger than 40 MΩ or if Rs changes by more than 20% during recording.
Apply a protocol delivering voltage pulses to step the membrane potential from −120 mV to +40 mV using 10 mV or 20 mV steps.
Record current responses to determine ion channel expression in the recorded cell.
Bath apply NMDA.
Keep NMDA on until a stable peak is reached or response begins to recover.
Wash out with recording aCSF if the cell responds.
Leave NMDA on for 4–5 minutes if the cell does not respond.
Bath apply kainate after acquiring a stable baseline post-NMDA application.
Keep kainate on until a stable peak is reached.
Capture an image of the Lucifer Yellow filled cell once recording is done.
Switch to the 4/5× objective to capture an image of the pipette location on the slice.
Record this information in your lab book.
Remove the electrode from the cell, trying to keep the cell intact in the slice.
Depolarize the cell to 0 mV if necessary.
For cells with high seal resistance (>10 GΩ), slowly pull the pipette away and upwards.
Observe a thread of membrane between the electrode and soma.
Detach the thread from the cell body if possible, leaving it intact in the slice.
If slow removal is insufficient, apply positive pressure or move the pipette sideways.
For persistent attachment, pull the pipette away quickly or gently tap the stage.
Note that long recordings may make it more difficult to retain the cell during electrode removal.
Repeat steps 12–30 if attempting the next cell on the same slice.
Change slices approximately every hour or after each cell when using drugs that are difficult to wash out or bind irreversibly.
Note the slice orientation in your lab book and make a mark on symmetrical slices for post-hoc immunohistochemistry.
Immediately fix the finished slice in 4% PFA in a 24-well plate at room temperature (19°C–23°C) on a rotating shaker, or overnight (10–20 h) at 4°C, on a rotating shaker.
Wash slices 3 × 30 min in PBS after fixing the slices.
Store fixed slices at 4°C in 0.05% NaN3 in PBS.
Perform immunohistochemistry within a week following patch clamp and slice fixation for best results.
Wash the slices for 15 minutes in PBS.
Incubate the slices in blocking solution at room temperature on a rotating shaker for 4 hours.
Incubate the slices with primary antibodies in PBS overnight at room temperature on a rotating shaker.
Wash slices 3 × 30 min in PBS.
Incubate the slices with secondary antibodies in PBS at room temperature (19°C–23°C) on a rotating shaker for 5 h.
Alternatively, incubate the secondary antibody overnight (10–20 h) at 4°C on a rotating shaker.
Wash slices 2 × 30 min in PBS.
Incubate with DAPI for 20 min.
Wash slices 30 min in PBS.
Mount the slices on glass microscope slides.
Image the patched cells using a confocal microscope.
Prepare a 7 mL universal tube per sample with 2 mL papain dissociation medium for adult brains or 1 mL for neonatal/embryonic brains.
Add L-cysteine to the papain dissociation medium and incubate for 10 min at 37°C.
Humanely sacrifice an animal in accordance with local regulations.
Dissect the brain as described in Preparing acute brain slices and place it, or the dissected region of interest, in a large weighing boat.
Quickly cut up the brain into small pieces using a scalpel.
Add tissue pieces to papain dissociation medium; pool 2-3 embryonic/neonatal brains in 1 mL medium.
Cut adult sample tissue into smaller pieces with scissors.
Incubate for 1 h at 37°C.
During incubation, prepare for myelin removal.
Cool the ovomuccoid, PBS, and BSA on ice.
Prepare 7 × 15 mL tubes per sample if using 3 columns per sample.
Prepare 1 × 50 mL tube per sample.
Inhibit digestion with 1 mL of ovomuccoid.
Resuspend the tissue and transfer to a 15 mL tube.
Complete the suspension to 8 mL with ovomuccoid.
Centrifuge for 10 minutes at 300 g.
Wash in 7 mL ice-cold PBS.
Proceed with myelin removal using Myltenyi Biotec Myelin Removal Beads II following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Filter the samples before adding the Myelin Removal Beads.
Use a 70 μm cell strainer between steps 2 and 3 of the magnetic labeling in the Myltenyi protocol.
Wait for the columns to be empty before applying the wash (step 4 of the depletion with LS columns).
Combine the flow-through from all columns used for the same sample.
Perform the myelin removal on ice.
Perform the procedure in a microbiological safety cabinet to preserve RNA.
Omit the myelin removal step for embryonic and neonatal samples.
Proceed with the OPC isolation using Miltenyi Biotec CD140 MicroBeads following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Perform the magnetic labeling by preparing MS columns, MiniMACS Separators, and MACS MultiStand during the first centrifugation step.
Remove the columns from the MiniMACS Separators before plunging them to collect the isolated OPCs.
Sort OPCs on ice in a microbiological safety cabinet.
Proceed with RNA extraction using Qiagen’s RNeasy Micro Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Include DNase when performing step 5 in the Qiagen protocol.
Avoid genomic DNA contamination by ensuring DNase is used during RNA extraction.
Add β-mercaptoethanol to buffer RLT.
Perform RNA extraction in a microbiological safety cabinet.
Store RNA at −80°C until all samples are processed.
Quantify the RNA concentration using a Qubit Fluorometer.
Measure the RNA Integrity Number (RIN) using an Agilent Bioanalyzer.
Prepare the RNA-seq library using Takara Clontech’s SMARTer Stranded Total RNA-seq Kit v2 - Pico Input Mammalian according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Sequence the libraries on an Illumina sequencer (or another appropriate instrument).
Assess read quality and trim the reads using standard protocols.
Align the reads to a reference mouse genome (such as GRCm38/mm10) using standard protocols.
Proceed with normalization and differential expression analysis with appropriate software and protocols.
Perform any other required analyses using appropriate software and protocols.
Use DAVID for GO term analysis.
Utilize REVIGO for gene ontology visualization.
